读法：它在地图上的位置很稳但很挤——下面被「免费捆绑」压（Teams / Google Chat）、侧面被「更轻更快」切（Discord、GroupMe）、上面被「更专业的项目管理」挡（Asana / Monday）。它唯一的空位是「跨组织协作 + 应用目录 + 双向 MCP」这个组合：前两个别人做不厚，第三个别人还没做。竞品价格本次全部未核验，不做价格对比。

extra_zh.title: 竞品技术底座
extra_zh.body:
AI 构建过程（Slack 怎么把原子拼成工作流）：① 先有 12 个原子——Channel / Canvas / List / Message / Huddle / App / Agent / Slackbot / Workflow / MCP tool / Search / 权限；② 再一条拼接公式——容器 × 身份 × 权限 × 触发器 × 工具 = 一个工作流（官方的四个例子：Channel+App+OAuth scope+事件+Web API、Channel+Agent+MCP tool+权限+@、Workflow(trigger)+条件+连接器+消息步骤、Huddle+AI 摘要+Canvas）；③ 最后三种封装——Template 给人、Slackbot Skills 给团队方法（markdown 或 canvas 写成指令 → 组织级发布）、Agent + 双向 MCP 给机器（Slack MCP Server 让外部 AI 读写 Slack，Slackbot MCP Client 让 Slack 调你的 server）。所以它的「AI」不是某个功能，而是「把任意业务动作变成频道里一次可被 @ 的调用」。下表先看它自己这一层，再看各家的底座能锁住什么。

产品底座它锁住了什么能力
Slack自建消息与权限模型（Channel / OAuth scope / Events / Block Kit）+ 双向 MCP（server 与 client 都做）+ 可插拔模型（自己不做基础模型，靠合作）锁住「身份 × 权限 × 上下文」这一层：任何人想让 agent 动真实业务数据，都绕不开它的授权与审计
Microsoft TeamsMicrosoft 365 的账号与图（Graph）体系，会议与文件同栈；AI 侧接 Copilot锁住「已经在付钱的企业」：AI 作为套餐的一部分出现，边际定价为零
Google ChatWorkspace 账号体系 + Gmail / Drive / Meet 同栈锁住「Workspace 客户的默认位」：不需要采购决策就能被用上
Discord频道 + 语音房的自建实时栈，为大规模并发与在场感优化锁住「社群与创作者」这一层的体验标准（延迟、在场、表情），但不锁治理
Mattermost开源 + 自托管，企业自己运维锁住「数据不出内网」这条硬约束——这是 SaaS 永远拿不到的一段市场
Asana / Monday / ClickUp结构化数据（任务/看板/字段）+ 自动化规则锁住「流程与责任」这一层：谁负责、卡在哪、什么时候交

[推断] 真护城河不在模型，也不在功能数量，在「谁持有授权链」。AI 时代的 agent 要动真实数据，必须过四道门：身份（它是谁）、权限（它能碰什么）、上下文（它看得懂什么）、审计（它做过什么）。Slack 把四道门全握在手里，这是它比「功能更多」更值钱的地方；Teams 与 Google Chat 握的是前三道的另一种版本（账号体系），第四道（审计与信息屏障）反而是 Slack 更细。
反过来说，它的底座有一个别人没有的弱点：它不拥有模型。上游模型能力一旦变成商品，它的 AI 差异化就只能靠封装与权限——这也解释了它为什么急着做双向 MCP：把「上下文」变成别人离不开的东西。

extra_zh.title: 可迁移的机会（我的判断）
extra_zh.body:
1. 把「Skills → 组织资产」抄成知识库产品——用 markdown 或画布写指令，创建 → 更新 → 组织级发布 → 入成员库，四步照抄；但只做一个窄场景（某岗位的固定流程）。为什么值得抄：绝大多数知识库停在「文档存起来」，Slack 走完了最后一步「能力被调用」。最轻，改的是发布机制不是数据模型。
  2. 先做协议/插件，不做又一个界面——把产品做成 MCP server + 一个 Skill 包，让 Claude、Cursor、Slackbot 都能当宿主。为什么：Slack 证明「定义好身份+权限+事件+消息格式，生态会替你长功能」；资源少的团队没有第二种拿到分发的方式。最快见效。
  3. 定价按「AI 执行量」分档，但把额度写明——Slack 已经把分档线从席位挪到 Slackbot 额度，却没公布数值；照抄方向、反着做透明度（额度、超额单价、用量面板、上限封顶），是最省力的差异化。
  4. 把「注意力路由」当第一职责——G2 里 5 星用户的最大不满是「重要的被埋了」。做任何消息型产品，AI 的第一件事应该是「判断这条要不要现在打扰谁」，而不是「再写一段摘要」。最难，但这是唯一能同时提升留存与口碑的方向。

四个里哪个最该先做？第 2 个：它不要求你有流量，只要求你把接口写对；哪个最容易被忽略？第 1 个——大家都把它当「模板功能」，其实它是「方法论市场」的地基。

extra_zh.title: 流量与变现拆解
extra_zh.body:
先把规模摊开（全部来自官方 sitemap 实测，2026-11-26）：营销站英文 1,769 页，13 个语种各一份（zh-CN 1,478 页）；其中 /blog/* 1,179 页是最大单一板块，/customer-stories/* 199 页，/resources/* 107 页，/templates/* 50 页，/solutions/* 32 页，/features/* 23 页。另有两套独立信息架构：Marketplace 2,881 页（2,871 个应用页 + 9 个合集 + 1 个首页）、帮助中心 579 页（578 篇 × 13 语言）。三套加起来，英文侧约 5,229 个可索引入口，再乘 12 个语种的重复。

环节它怎么做的为什么有效 / 哪里漏
拉新13 语种大站 + 2,881 页应用目录 + 579 页帮助中心 + 2 个产品级对比页 + 18 条博客对比集群有效：页面规模本身就是壁垒，长尾词全覆盖。漏点：sitemap 只能证明页面存在，不能证明流量；自然搜索占比本次未核验
激活所有页面 CTA 是 Get started（无销售介入）；模板可一键落进工作区；免费档即含 AI 摘要与 Slackbot 试用有效：试用零摩擦。漏点：90 天历史 + 10 个 app 的墙会让小团队在「刚用顺」时撞上付费
留存频道历史 + 线程 + Canvas/List + 2,600 应用的集成位 + 治理策略有效：四层叠起来迁移成本极高。漏点：留存的是组织，不是个人——个人对它的黏性远低于组织
变现Free $0 / Pro $8.75（年付 $7.25）/ Business+ $18（年付 $15）/ Enterprise+ $45（仅年付）有效：付费点全部落在「组织变大才需要」的东西上。漏点：AI 额度不公布，采购算不出账
扩张席位随人数增长；Connect 从跨部门长到跨公司；Slackbot 额度与 Flex Credits 按 AI 用量计价[推断] 扩张的真实阻力不是价格，是「治理先行」：信息屏障与法定保留一旦是硬要求，决策周期就从一个人点一下变成 IT 与法务排队

套利三问。钱从谁的兜里出：企业 IT / 业务部门的年度预算，个人几乎不付费——免费档就是给个人用的。还能拿多久：[推断] 只要「跨组织协作」与「应用目录」还是它的独占资产，就能一直拿；但 AI 这一层的溢价窗口在收窄（捆绑品免费送）。凭什么你拿到：靠三件别人短期补不齐的东西——2,600 个按它的权限模型写好的应用、跨公司网络、治理颗粒度。

最脆的那根梁：「工作发生在频道里」这个前提。如果 agent 时代的人不再关心「在哪儿说」（直接跟 agent 说），那么它 2,881 页的应用目录、13 语种的 SEO、甚至治理层，都会从「资产」变成「一层昂贵的中间件」。它现在的解法是双向 MCP——让自己成为 agent 必经的路，而不是 agent 的替代品。这条路对不对，2026 年还看不出来。

extra_en.title: Competitive map
extra_en.body:
This list is not guesswork; it comes from Slack's own moves. Product-level comparison pages are only two (/compare/slack-vs-teams, /compare/slack-vs-email), but the blog cluster /blog/compare/* holds 18 — 13 competitor-vs pages (asana, chatwork, clickup, discord, google-chat, line-works, mattermost, microsoft-teams, monday, stackfield, trello, whatsapp, zoom) plus 4 alternatives pages (teams / discord / google-chat / trello) and one German legal page. In other words: who it counts as a rival is written in its blog directory.

WhoFighting for the same needFighting for the same link in the chainWhere users actually go
Microsoft TeamsThe same enterprise employees: companies already on Microsoft 365The same entry point: chat + meetings + files inside one Microsoft 365 accountIts only product-level comparison target (/compare/slack-vs-teams). The threat isn't features, it's 'we already paid for this'
Google ChatWorkspace customers: teams already on Gmail / Drive / MeetThe same entry: mail, docs and meetings in one stack, where the account is the permissionIt runs /blog/compare/slack-vs-google-chat plus a google-chat-alternatives page — active defence
DiscordCommunities and hobby groups first, now seeping into small-team workChannels plus voice rooms for presence, without governanceG2 reviewers recommend GroupMe or lighter chat tools, which shows the 'I just want chat' segment leaking away
Mattermost / Stackfield / Chatwork / Line WorksOrganisations whose data can't leave the intranet, or whose local market is held by a local productSelf-hosted and localised deployment; trading features for data staying homeAll four appear in its blog competitor list: these are its defence targets in public sector and regional markets
Asana / Trello / Monday / ClickUpTeams that need projects tracked, not conversations seenThe task-and-process link in the chain (Slack answers with Lists + Workflow Builder)Four separate vs pages. Its answer isn't a better project tool but moving the project into the channel (Lists + templates)
ZoomMeeting-first teamsThe meeting link in the chain (Slack answers with Huddles)Has /blog/compare/slack-vs-zoom — the collision of meeting tools moving into chat and chat tools moving into meetings

How to read the map: its position is secure but crowded — pressed from below by free bundling (Teams / Google Chat), cut from the side by lighter and faster tools (Discord, GroupMe), and blocked from above by deeper project management (Asana / Monday). Its only open slot is the combination of cross-org collaboration + app directory + bidirectional MCP: nobody else has the first two at this thickness, and nobody has shipped the third. Competitor prices were not verified this round, so no price comparison is offered.

extra_en.title: Rivals' technical base
extra_en.body:
How the AI is built (turning atoms into workflows): (1) twelve atoms — Channel / Canvas / List / Message / Huddle / App / Agent / Slackbot / Workflow / MCP tool / Search / permissions; (2) one composition formula — container × identity × permissions × trigger × tool = a workflow (the four examples the company itself uses: Channel+App+OAuth scope+events+Web API, Channel+Agent+MCP tool+permissions+@, Workflow(trigger)+conditions+connector+message step, Huddle+AI summary+Canvas); (3) three wrappers — a Template for people, Slackbot Skills for team method (write instructions in markdown or a canvas, publish at org level), and Agent + bidirectional MCP for machines (Slack MCP Server lets external AI read and write Slack; Slackbot MCP Client lets Slack call your server). So its 'AI' is not a feature — it is turning any business action into one @-able call inside a channel. The table below reads its own layer first, then what each rival's base locks up.

ProductBaseWhat that base locks up
SlackIts own messaging and permission model (Channel / OAuth scopes / Events / Block Kit) + bidirectional MCP (server and client) + pluggable models (it does not build foundation models, it partners)Locks up the identity × permission × context layer: anyone who wants an agent to touch real business data has to go through its authorisation and audit
Microsoft TeamsThe Microsoft 365 account and graph, with meetings and files on the same stack; AI arrives as CopilotLocks up 'enterprises that already pay': AI appears as part of a bundle, with zero marginal pricing
Google ChatThe Workspace account system with Gmail / Drive / Meet on the same stackLocks up 'the Workspace default': it gets used without a procurement decision
DiscordA self-built realtime stack of channels and voice rooms, optimised for concurrency and presenceLocks up the experience standard for communities and creators (latency, presence, reactions) but not governance
MattermostOpen source, self-hosted, operated by the customerLocks up 'data never leaves the intranet' — a segment SaaS can never reach
Asana / Monday / ClickUpStructured data (tasks, boards, fields) plus automation rulesLocks up the process-and-accountability layer: who owns it, where it's stuck, when it's due

[inferred] The real moat is not the model and not the feature count — it is who holds the authorisation chain. An agent touching real data has to pass four gates: identity (who it is), permission (what it may touch), context (what it understands) and audit (what it did). Slack holds all four, which is worth more than having more features; Teams and Google Chat hold a different version of the first three (the account system), and the fourth — audit and information barriers — is actually finer-grained at Slack.
The flip side is a weakness nobody else has: Slack does not own a model. Once upstream model capability becomes a commodity, its AI differentiation rests entirely on packaging and permissions — which is exactly why it rushed bidirectional MCP: to turn 'context' into something others can't leave.

extra_en.title: Portable opportunities (my judgement)
extra_en.body:
1. Copy 'Skills → organisational asset' as a knowledge product — instructions in markdown or a canvas, then create → update → org-level publish → member library, four steps copied wholesale, but landing in one narrow scenario (a role's fixed process). Why it's worth copying: most knowledge products stop at 'the document is stored'; Slack finished the last step, 'the capability gets called'. Lightest option — it changes publishing, not the data model.
  2. Build the protocol/plugin first, not another interface — ship as an MCP server plus a Skill pack so Claude, Cursor and Slackbot can all be hosts. Why: Slack proved that defining identity, permissions, events and message format makes the ecosystem grow features for you, and a small team has no second route to distribution. Fastest to show results.
  3. Price by AI execution, but publish the allowance — Slack already moved the tier line from seats to Slackbot allowance without publishing the numbers. Copy the direction and invert the transparency (allowance, overage price, usage dashboard, hard cap): the cheapest differentiation on the table.
  4. Make attention routing the first job — the loudest complaint among 5-star G2 reviewers is that important things get buried. For any message-shaped product, the AI's first act should be deciding whether this deserves to interrupt anyone now, not writing another summary. Hardest, and the only direction that lifts retention and reputation at once.

Which of the four first? Number 2 — it doesn't require traffic, only that you get the interface right. Which gets ignored? Number 1 — everyone files it under 'templates', when it is really the foundation of a marketplace of methods.

extra_en.title: Traffic and monetisation
extra_en.body:
First, the scale, all from official sitemaps measured on 2026-11-26: the English marketing site holds 1,769 URLs replicated across 13 languages (zh-CN 1,478); within it /blog/* at 1,179 pages is the largest single block, then /customer-stories/* 199, /resources/* 107, /templates/* 50, /solutions/* 32, /features/* 23. Two further architectures run separately: Marketplace 2,881 pages (2,871 app pages + 9 collections + 1 index) and the Help Center at 579 pages (578 × 13 languages). Together that is roughly 5,229 indexable English entry points, multiplied again across 12 other languages.

StageWhat it doesWhy it works / where it leaks
AcquisitionA 13-language mega-site + a 2,881-page app directory + 579 help pages + 2 product comparison pages + an 18-page blog comparison clusterWorks: page scale is itself a barrier and the long tail is fully covered. Leak: a sitemap proves pages exist, not traffic; organic share was not verified this round
ActivationEvery page CTA is 'Get started' with no sales gate; templates drop into a workspace in one click; AI summaries and a Slackbot trial are already in the free tierWorks: zero-friction trial. Leak: the 90-day history and 10-app walls hit small teams right when they get fluent
RetentionChannel history + threads + Canvas/Lists + 2,600 integration slots + governance policiesWorks: four layers make migration brutal. Leak: it retains the organisation, not the individual — personal stickiness is far lower
MonetisationFree $0 / Pro $8.75 (annual $7.25) / Business+ $18 (annual $15) / Enterprise+ $45 (annual only)Works: every paywall sits on something only a bigger org needs. Leak: AI allowance unpublished, so procurement can't do the maths
ExpansionSeats grow with headcount; Connect grows from cross-department to cross-company; Slackbot allowance and Flex Credits price AI by usage[inferred] The real brake isn't price, it's governance-first: once information barriers and legal hold are hard requirements, the cycle goes from one click to IT plus legal

The three arbitrage questions. Whose pocket does the money come from: enterprise IT and departmental budgets — individuals barely pay, the free tier is for them. How long can it keep taking it: [inferred] as long as cross-org collaboration and the app directory stay exclusive; the AI premium window, however, is narrowing as bundled products give it away. Why does it get it: three things rivals can't assemble quickly — 2,600 apps written against its permission model, the cross-company network, and governance granularity.

The weakest beam: the premise that work happens in a channel. If agent-era users stop caring where they said something and just talk to an agent, then its 2,881-page directory, its 13-language SEO and even its governance layer turn from assets into expensive middleware. Its current answer is bidirectional MCP — making itself the road every agent must travel rather than a replacement for the agent. Whether that road holds is not visible from 2026.
